options_ranked.title: Renewal-Led Synthetic Blend Price Recovery
options_ranked.description: Reset Synthetic Blend Engine Oil pricing only at legally permitted renewal or reset dates, using substantiated performance differentiation, discount floors and contractually permitted input-cost indexation. Pair signed renewals with supplier term improvements for the same demand, while keeping pricing as the primary mechanism. Target Synthetic Blend at 20.64% versus 27.78%; extend discount discipline to Conventional Engine Oil and Value accounts only where their contracts permit. Do not impose mid-quarter list-price increases on anchor accounts. Preserve practices in periods 2026-006, 2026-007 and 2026-008 classified within threshold; no well-performing product segment is identified for broader intervention or benchmark replication.
options_ranked.rationale: Synthetic Blend's 7.14-point decline provides a specific recovery target, and the confirmed net_revenue-to-gross-margin relationship supports realized-price improvement as a direct mechanism. Renewal timing respects the anchor-account lock, but neither renewal coverage nor customer willingness to pay is established. The supplier component is conditional commercial upside, not a claim that hedging itself reduces costs; the full range requires both components.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 3–12 months, beginning at the first legally permitted contract reset

arguments_for: Price-volume-mix decomposition supports improving realized price on Synthetic Blend without relying on an unverified premium-mix benefit; the product currently earns 20.64% margin.
arguments_against: Customer profitability and willingness-to-pay segmentation cannot establish a 2–3-point price contribution from the supplied evidence because renewal coverage, elasticity and discount leakage are not quantified.
key_questions: Which permitted renewals can support margin floors without reducing customer-level gross profit through lost volume?

arguments_for: Matching supplier commitments to renewed demand can reduce procurement mismatch, and the client-confirmed COGS identity supports margin improvement when actual input cost falls.
arguments_against: Procurement hedges protect against future volatility but do not establish the proposed 1.5–2.5-point cost recovery; unfavorable commitments could offset price gains.
key_questions: Will signed supplier terms produce actual net landed-cost savings after financing, inventory and hedge costs?

arguments_for: A renewal-based intervention tests whether Synthetic Blend participation remains attractive before withdrawing from a product that currently outperforms Conventional Engine Oil by 1.48 margin points.
arguments_against: Portfolio participation analysis warns that repeated renewal concessions could preserve demand whose avoidable contribution is inadequate, even if reported margin improves.
key_questions: What minimum retained-account contribution will trigger non-renewal instead of another pricing concession?

implementation_triggers: A contract reaches a legally permitted reset date and the approved offer preserves customer-level contribution after a realistic volume response.
Supplier terms offer positive net landed-cost savings on committed renewal demand; otherwise exclude that component from the executable business case.
An account rejects the contribution floor, triggering escalation for service redesign or non-renewal rather than an unauthorized price increase.
prerequisites: Legal clearance of renewal dates, notice requirements and discount changes; no circumvention of the mid-quarter list-price lock.
Sales-approved account offers with substantiated durability or certification claims and explicit walk-away contribution floors.
Separate ownership of price and procurement savings so benefits are not counted twice with the procurement alternative.
Use existing contract and cost records to execute offers; do not make a new analytics program the intervention.

impact_estimate.basis: The Stage 1 scenario combines 2–3 percentage points from renewal pricing with 1.5–2.5 points from supplier improvements against Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline, implying segment margin of 24.14–26.14% rather than an enterprise recovery.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend has a 7.14-point segment margin gap available for partial recovery.
key_assumptions.provenance: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil change point: 20.64% current versus 27.78% previous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Approximately 60–70% of relevant customer exposure can renew within the next two quarters.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed renewals cover 60–70% of the relevant revenue exposure within two quarters; Stage 1 supplies this as an assumption, not an observed contract fact.

key_assumptions.assumption: Renewal offers can deliver 2–3 segment margin points without contribution-destroying volume loss.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed renewal prices, retained volumes and rebates produce a net 2–3-point contribution to Synthetic Blend margin.

key_assumptions.assumption: Supplier improvements can add 1.5–2.5 segment margin points independently of renewal pricing.
key_assumptions.provenance: Supplier invoices and landed-cost settlements show incremental savings equivalent to 1.5–2.5% of Synthetic Blend revenue, excluding price benefits and hedge valuation gains.

flagged_side_effects: Renewal price increases may cause customer attrition or channel switching, reducing gross profit despite a higher margin percentage.
Forward purchasing can increase working capital and leave inventory exposed if renewed demand falls.

options_ranked.title: Qualified Synthetic Blend Cost-Down and Procurement Protection
options_ranked.description: Negotiate supplier rebates and lower landed-cost terms for Synthetic Blend inputs, qualify formulation changes that preserve performance specifications, and use limited 60–90-day procurement protection only for committed exposure. Start with existing approved alternatives; do not reduce additive intensity or substitute base stocks before technical and customer approvals. Target Synthetic Blend first, with Conventional Engine Oil eligible for reuse of technically applicable purchasing improvements. Preserve within-threshold practices in periods 2026-006, 2026-007 and 2026-008; no named healthy product benchmark is available. Keep customer list prices unchanged during anchor-account locks.
options_ranked.rationale: The client-confirmed base-oil-cost-to-COGS component relationship and COGS-to-Gross-Margin-% identity support actual cost reduction without violating pricing locks. Parallel product declines are consistent with, but do not establish, common input pressure. Procurement protection is downside insurance rather than recovery of historical inflation, so the required recovery anchor remains an unsubstantiated stretch scenario until executable supplier and engineering savings bridge the arithmetic gap.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 0–90 days for supplier terms and already-qualified changes; longer for formulations requiring new certification

arguments_for: Cost-to-serve improvement protects contribution while anchor-account prices remain locked, avoiding reliance on customer acceptance of an immediate increase.
arguments_against: Willingness-to-pay economics can deteriorate if formulation changes weaken performance claims or customer confidence, offsetting the purchasing benefit.
key_questions: Which changes retain the specifications and claims embedded in current customer contracts?

arguments_for: Bottom-up cost reduction uses the confirmed base oil, manufacturing, distribution and packaging components of COGS, making invoice and production savings distinguishable from allocation changes.
arguments_against: At the current 20.64% margin, COGS equals 79.36% of revenue; a 2–3% COGS reduction cannot independently deliver the proposed 3.5–5.8-point recovery.
key_questions: Which signed savings beyond the engineering reduction close the gap without counting avoided future inflation as current recovery?

arguments_for: An initially narrow cost-down program preserves participation choices and can establish whether existing Synthetic Blend demand can earn adequate contribution under locked prices.
arguments_against: Portfolio economics can worsen if long supplier commitments entrench production for accounts that remain unattractive after the cost reduction.
key_questions: What commitment limits prevent purchasing savings from locking the business into uneconomic demand?

implementation_triggers: A supplier offers positive net landed-cost savings without commitments exceeding conservatively committed demand.
A formulation change passes technical, certification and customer-approval gates before any production release.
Treasury approves a suitable instrument, exposure limit and basis-risk treatment before any hedge is executed.
Stop rollout if field performance, supply continuity or net savings fails the approved release thresholds.
prerequisites: Quality-approved specifications and production-release authority for every formulation change.
Treasury policy covering counterparty, liquidity, basis risk and accounting treatment; use fixed-price supply contracts where suitable derivatives are unavailable.
Procurement contracts that separate rebates and actual cost reductions from volatility protection.
Finance sign-off on the executable savings bridge before treating the mandated recovery range as a budget commitment.

impact_estimate.basis: The mandated Stage 1 range represents approximately 49–81% of Synthetic Blend Engine Oil's 7.14-point decline and would lift its margin to 24.14–26.44%, but the proposed 2–3% unit-COGS reduction alone supports only about 1.59–2.38 points at unchanged revenue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Lower actual base oil cost reduces COGS and improves Gross Margin % at unchanged revenue.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed causal context identifies base oil as a COGS component and COGS as an input to Gross Margin %.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil inflation is a material cause of the observed Synthetic Blend decline.
key_assumptions.provenance: Existing purchase-price and consumption records attribute a material portion of the 7.14-point loss to base oil rather than discounts, absorption or other costs.

key_assumptions.assumption: Qualified engineering changes can reduce unit COGS by 2–3% without weakening product performance.
key_assumptions.provenance: Released production batches achieve a 2–3% unit-cost reduction and pass all required specification and customer acceptance tests.

key_assumptions.assumption: Procurement savings beyond engineering can bridge the remaining recovery requirement.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed supplier concessions deliver enough incremental savings to bridge the difference between the 1.59–2.38-point engineering contribution and the 3.5–5.8-point scenario.

key_assumptions.assumption: Short-duration procurement protection has acceptable basis risk and liquidity demands.
key_assumptions.provenance: Treasury-approved exposures remain within liquidity and basis-risk limits through settlement.

flagged_side_effects: Unqualified formulation changes could compromise certification, warranties and customer retention.
Hedges can lock in unfavorable prices or generate liquidity demands; they do not guarantee lower COGS.
Lower accounting allocations without lower total spending would overstate economic savings.

options_ranked.title: Gated Portfolio Reallocation with Avoidable-Cost Removal
options_ranked.description: Replace the proposed audit-led approach with selective non-renewal or service redesign of weak-contribution Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil business, removal of avoidable production and delivery costs, and customer-approved reallocation only to demonstrably superior alternatives. Do not shift toward Conventional Engine Oil: its 19.16% margin is below Synthetic Blend's 20.64%. Compressor Oil has a higher current margin of 28%, but it is also underperforming by 5.86 points and is not assumed to be a substitute; first restore its avoidable contribution through executable cost and service changes, then allow only technically compatible demand migration. High Mileage and specialty synthetics are not authorized destinations because their margins are absent. Preserve within-threshold periods 2026-006, 2026-007 and 2026-008; no healthy product benchmark is supplied.
options_ranked.rationale: Portfolio participation analysis addresses whether unattractive demand should remain in the business rather than assuming every product's prior margin must be restored. The confirmed revenue and COGS identities support the mechanism, but aggregate uplift requires revenue weights, avoidable costs and customer-compatible alternatives that are not supplied. Reallocation is gated on actual destination margins and total gross profit because reducing Synthetic Blend could reduce premium mix; the premium-mix benefit is an unconfirmed industry prior, not an established fact.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 0–90 days for service redesign and avoidable-cost removal; 3–12 months for contract-permitted portfolio migration

arguments_for: Customer profitability analysis supports withdrawing concessions or redesigning service for accounts that remain unattractive after feasible cost reductions.
arguments_against: Customer and channel economics may deteriorate if engine-oil reductions cause loss of profitable bundled purchases; neither bundle contribution nor migration acceptance is quantified.
key_questions: Which customers can accept the proposed product or service change without reducing total retained-account contribution?

arguments_for: Avoidable-cost removal through shipment consolidation and production simplification can reduce distribution or manufacturing COGS through client-confirmed component relationships.
arguments_against: Overhead absorption diagnostics warn that withdrawing volume can strand fixed costs and increase remaining unit costs; removing allocated cost is not equivalent to eliminating cash spending.
key_questions: Which contracts, shifts, freight movements or inventory commitments will actually disappear when the targeted volume is withdrawn?

arguments_for: Portfolio participation analysis supports explicit renewal and exit thresholds rather than indefinite support for demand that cannot cover avoidable costs under contractual constraints.
arguments_against: Category lifecycle analysis cannot establish structural decline from one year-to-date comparison, and the proposed destinations lack sufficient evidence of sustainable superior economics.
key_questions: What signed destination business and removable costs must exist before any irreversible withdrawal is released?

implementation_triggers: An account reaches a contract-permitted exit or service-change date and remains below its approved contribution floor after feasible mitigation.
A destination has a verified higher realized margin and better incremental contribution after switching, service and stranded-cost effects.
For any underperforming destination, its approved cost or service correction is operational before migration accelerates.
No volume transfer proceeds unless customer technical suitability and non-negative total gross-profit impact are signed off.
prerequisites: Legal approval of service obligations and exit notices; no mid-quarter anchor-account list-price increase or unilateral breach of committed supply.
CFO approval of the SKU-level margin and mix bridge using existing records before each migration, explicitly including the possible loss of premium mix.
Operations commitment to specific avoidable-cost removals rather than merely reallocating overhead.
Commercial confirmation of customer-compatible destinations; do not assume Compressor Oil can replace engine oil.
Treat the mandated enterprise range as an unverified scenario, not a spending authorization or additive benefit alongside the other alternatives.

impact_estimate.basis: The mandated Stage 1 blended-margin scenario combines targeted cost removal and portfolio reallocation, but its 2.8–4.5-point enterprise recovery is not supported by supplied revenue weights and its upper bound exceeds the observed 4.49-point aggregate decline by 0.01 point.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conventional Engine Oil is not a superior current-margin destination for Synthetic Blend volume.
key_assumptions.provenance: Current product margins are 19.16% for Conventional Engine Oil and 20.64% for Synthetic Blend Engine Oil.

key_assumptions.assumption: Compressor Oil has a higher current margin but also requires remediation.
key_assumptions.provenance: Compressor Oil current margin is 28% versus 33.86% previously, a 5.86-point decline.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customer-compatible destinations can absorb economically meaningful demand at better realized contribution.
key_assumptions.provenance: Customer-approved migration orders show higher incremental contribution after qualification, switching and delivery costs.

key_assumptions.assumption: Withdrawal of selected business releases sufficient actual costs to offset stranded overhead and lost gross profit.
key_assumptions.provenance: Executed supplier cancellations, shipment reductions and production changes lower total spending enough to preserve or increase total gross profit.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reducing Synthetic Blend participation does not create a net adverse premium-mix effect.
key_assumptions.provenance: The approved migration bridge and subsequent realized results show no net margin loss from reduced Synthetic Blend participation; the supplied premium-mix relationship is an unconfirmed industry prior.

key_assumptions.assumption: Portfolio weights are large enough for the mandated enterprise recovery scenario.
key_assumptions.provenance: Approved revenue-weighted migration economics support enterprise margin uplift after all retained and exited business is included.

flagged_side_effects: Reducing Synthetic Blend may lower premium mix and erase some intended margin benefit; require a positive realized SKU-margin and gross-profit bridge before migration.
Product withdrawal can strand fixed costs, weaken customer bundles and reduce total gross profit even as Gross Margin % rises.

commercial.framework: Price-Volume-Mix Decomposition with Customer Profitability Lens
commercial.hypothesis: Gross margin compression in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (−7.14pp) and Conventional Engine Oil (−6.61pp) is driven by a combination of elevated base oil input costs (COGS driver) and/or aggressive discounting on Value-tier products (−6.42pp category delta), masking any premium mix benefit. The 'Value' category decline suggests either forced repricing downward to maintain volume in a cost-inflationary environment, or loss of pricing power on anchor SKUs.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%) year-to-date, the largest single product driver, indicating concentrated pressure on the highest-margin formulation
Value product category declined 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), consistent with volume-preservation discounting on lower-tier SKUs that typically anchor customer contracts

Three products (Synthetic Blend, Conventional, Compressor Oil) all declined by 5.86–7.14pp within the same period, suggesting a common upstream cost shock (base oil, freight, or manufacturing) rather than product-specific demand loss

operational.framework: Cost-to-Serve Analysis with Input-Cost Hedging Diagnostics
operational.hypothesis: Base oil cost inflation (unhedged commodity exposure) is the primary driver of the 7.14 pp gross margin decline in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil YTD. The product carries the highest delta (-7.14 pp) and sits at the intersection of elevated raw material sensitivity and constrained pricing power (contractual price-lock on anchor accounts). A 15–25% rise in base oil feedstock costs, unabsorbed through either procurement hedging or price recovery, would mechanically produce a margin compression of this magnitude.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14 pp (27.78% → 20.64%), the largest single-product contributor, while Conventional Engine Oil fell 6.61 pp—both synthetic/blend formulations are base-oil-cost-sensitive and lack pricing flexibility under contractual lock.

Value product_category (delta -6.42 pp) overlaps heavily with engine oil SKUs; the concentration of margin loss in lower-tier, cost-sensitive segments is consistent with input-cost pass-through failure rather than volume or mix shift.
Compressor Oil (delta -5.86 pp) shows parallel pressure, suggesting a commodity-wide base oil cost shock affecting the entire lubricant portfolio, not a product-specific demand or operational issue.

structural.framework: Portfolio Participation Analysis + Category Lifecycle Positioning
structural.hypothesis: Gross margin compression across engine oil portfolio (Synthetic Blend -7.14pp, Conventional -6.61pp) signals structural cost inflation in base oil and/or distribution, not cyclical pricing variance. The simultaneous decline across both premium and value tiers, combined with the Value category decline (-6.42pp), suggests input-cost pass-through resistance rather than mix degradation or demand elasticity. Given contractual price-lock constraints, the margin gap is being absorbed in COGS, not recovered in pricing.
key_evidence: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil margin fell 7.14pp (27.78% → 20.64%), the largest single-product delta, indicating the highest-margin SKU is under cost pressure despite typically carrying structural margin protection
Conventional Engine Oil margin fell 6.61pp (25.77% → 19.16%), tracking within 0.53pp of Synthetic Blend decline, suggesting category-wide cost driver rather than product-specific mix shift

Value category margin fell 6.42pp (26.24% → 19.82%), nearly identical to both product-level declines, confirming the compression is portfolio-wide and resistant to premium/value segmentation—hallmark of raw material or logistics cost inflation

opt_1.causal_grounding: Confirmed net_revenue -> gross_margin_pct through realized-price changes; client-confirmed base_oil_cost -> cogs -> gross_margin_pct supports actual supplier cost reductions, but does not establish historical input inflation.

opt_2.grade_rationale: The intervention leaves anchor-account list prices unchanged, surviving the contractual lock, and actual cost-down follows the confirmed COGS mechanism. Renewal-cycle pricing allows list-price recovery on new terms without breaching existing contracts. Value-add positioning (durability, OEM spec compliance) justifies premium pricing relative to Conventional, recovering mix margin naturally. Forward procurement hedging reduces COGS volatility, lifting margin floor independent of price action.

proposed_option.title: Implement Dynamic Procurement Hedging & Selective SKU Cost-Down Engineering
proposed_option.description: Establish a 60–90 day rolling base oil futures hedge program (2–3 month forward contracts) to lock in feedstock costs and stabilize COGS predictability. In parallel, conduct rapid cost-down engineering on Synthetic Blend formulations: evaluate synthetic base stock substitution (PAO vs. Group II mineral), reduce additive package intensity where performance specs permit, and negotiate volume rebates with suppliers given YTD volume concentration. These moves target the unhedged commodity exposure without breaching the contractual price-lock constraint on anchor accounts.
proposed_option.mechanism: Hedging reduces the volatility of base oil input costs in COGS, protecting margin from further commodity shocks. Cost-down engineering lowers the absolute COGS per unit on Synthetic Blend SKUs, directly improving gross margin % even if net revenue remains constrained by pricing locks. Together, they address the supply-side cost structure rather than relying on commercial price recovery (which is contractually blocked mid-quarter).

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend margin delta of -7.14 pp assumes unrecovered base oil cost inflation of ~18–22% YTD. Hedging 60% of exposure and cost-down engineering of 2–3% per unit COGS would recover 50–80% of the observed decline (3.5–5.8 pp). Recovery is capped at 5.8 pp (81% of -7.14) to reflect implementation lag and partial hedging coverage.

proposed_option.title: Cost-Structure Audit & Selective SKU Reallocation to Mitigate Base Oil Inflation
proposed_option.description: Conduct rapid forensic breakdown of COGS components (base oil cost, manufacturing, distribution, packaging) for Synthetic Blend and Conventional oils to isolate which cost line is driving the 6.5–7.1pp margin erosion. Simultaneously, identify lower-margin SKUs or customer segments where volume can be redirected to higher-margin formulations (e.g., High Mileage or specialty synthetics) that may have smaller absolute cost inflation exposure, or where contractual flexibility exists to recover pricing. This reframes the problem from 'fix the margin on locked SKUs' to 'rebalance portfolio participation away from cost-inflated categories.'
proposed_option.mechanism: By isolating which cost component (base oil procurement, freight, manufacturing overhead) is the primary driver, the team can pursue targeted mitigation: (1) base oil cost → negotiate longer-term supplier contracts or hedge; (2) distribution cost → consolidate shipments or shift to lower-cost logistics partners for lower-tier products; (3) manufacturing → identify efficiency gains or shift production to lower-cost facilities. Simultaneously, reallocation of volume away from Synthetic Blend (where cost inflation is hitting the highest-margin product hardest) to SKUs with contractual pricing flexibility or lower cost-of-goods ratio reduces the blended portfolio margin drag without violating price-lock constraints.

impact_estimate.basis: If cost audit isolates base oil inflation as 40–60% of the 6.5–7.1pp decline, targeted procurement renegotiation could recover 0.8–1.2pp. Portfolio reallocation (shifting 15–25% of Synthetic Blend volume to higher-flex SKUs or lower-cost-ratio products) could recover an additional 2.0–3.3pp blended margin through mix optimization. Combined recovery: 2.8–4.5pp, leaving structural margin gap to be managed through longer-term pricing or category exit decisions.
